title: Search Console After Launch: A 28-Day Review for Small-Business Websites
description: Review a new or redesigned small-business website in Google Search Console without treating early impressions, indexing or average position as guaranteed results.
summary: A practical 28-day Search Console review for checking important pages, interpreting early query signals and choosing the next useful website action.
body:
A website launch gives you a new version to inspect, not an immediate verdict on search performance. Google still needs to discover, crawl, process and sometimes index the pages. Early Search Console rows can help you find technical problems and unexpected query matches, but a handful of impressions cannot establish demand or a ranking trend.

This review is for a small business launching a first website or completing a redesign. It turns the first 28 days into a sequence of checks: confirm the intended pages are available, understand what Google reports, and make changes only when the evidence points to a clear problem.

Record the intended website before reading the reports

Begin with the website you approved. List the canonical homepage, core service pages, contact or booking destination and any useful guides that should be public. Record old URLs that were redirected during a redesign and pages that should remain private or excluded.

Confirm each important public URL returns the expected page, has a descriptive title and one clear main heading, links into the visitor journey and names its canonical URL correctly. Test the contact or booking route separately. Search visibility is not useful when the visitor reaches a broken next step.

Include the intended canonical URLs in the XML sitemap and submit that sitemap through the verified property. Google’s sitemap documentation explains that a sitemap is a hint about preferred URLs; submission does not guarantee crawling, indexing or search appearance.

In the first week, check availability and indexability

Use URL Inspection for a small set of important pages rather than repeatedly requesting every URL. Google’s URL Inspection documentation separates information about Google’s indexed version from a live test of the current page. A live test can show whether the current version appears indexable, but it does not mean the page has entered the index.

Check the evidence before choosing an action
Report signalQuestion to answerUseful next action
URL is unknown to GoogleIs it linked from the public website and included in the current sitemap?Repair discovery paths, then inspect the exact canonical URL.
Crawling or indexing is blockedIs the robots rule, access control or noindex directive intentional?Correct an accidental block; preserve an intentional exclusion.
Google chose another canonicalAre duplicate URLs, redirects and canonical tags giving consistent signals?Review the URL group before changing content or requesting indexing.
Discovered or crawled, not indexedIs this an important, original page that serves a distinct visitor task?Check the reported reason and page usefulness; avoid repeated requests without a change.
IndexedDoes the indexed URL and canonical match the approved page?Move to query, page and enquiry review; indexing alone is not a result.

The Page indexing report guidance says that not every known URL should be indexed. Redirects, duplicates, removed pages and deliberately excluded paths can appear as not indexed for valid reasons. Review important canonical pages and the reason attached to each group instead of chasing a 100% coverage number.

Read early performance metrics as definitions, not promises

In the Search results performance report, an impression means a link to the property or page was shown under Google’s counting rules. A click records a click from a search result. Average position is an aggregate of the topmost position reported for the selected property or page across its impressions.

Google’s click, impression and position definitions explain that position varies by query and context. A property-wide average is not the permanent rank of every page. Use it to notice patterns over comparable periods, not as a number to reproduce with your own searches.

Switch between the Queries and Pages tables. A query row tells you language that produced reported visibility; a page row tells you which URL Google showed. The totals and visible rows may not add up exactly because some query data is omitted for privacy and because aggregation changes how metrics are counted. Google documents the difference between property and page aggregation.

Ask four questions at the end of 28 days

  1. Are the important pages eligible and discoverable? Review inspection evidence, sitemap processing, internal links and the indexing reason for the approved canonical URLs.
  2. Are relevant queries matching the intended page? Group close wording by buyer intent. Improve one useful canonical page when several variations ask for the same service.
  3. Is the search snippet accurate enough to earn a suitable click? Review the title, description and visible page promise together. Do not write a sensational title that the page cannot fulfil.
  4. Does the page support a qualified next step? Test the call, WhatsApp, email or booking journey and review actual received enquiries separately from Search Console clicks.

Use one completed period as a baseline and compare it with a later period of the same length. Record deployments and material content changes, otherwise a chart movement has no useful context. A new property with sparse data may need more time before a comparison supports a decision.

Hypothetical example: a Varanasi home-repair website

Imagine a fictional Varanasi home-repair business launches a homepage, three genuine service pages and a contact page. This is a planning example, not a SiteSutra client or performance result.

During the first-week review, the approved service pages pass live inspection, but one old URL still appears in the indexing report. The redirect inventory shows that the old URL should lead to the closest current service page. The owner tests that destination and records the redirect rather than creating another page to preserve the obsolete address.

By the end of the first completed review period, Search Console reports a few relevant impressions for one service page and an unrelated query for the services overview. The team strengthens the useful service page with confirmed inclusions, coverage information and a working enquiry route. It ignores the unrelated query because the business does not provide that service.

The team does not create separate pages for every close wording such as “repair company,” “repair service” and “home repair help.” Those variations belong on the maintained service page when they express the same buyer need. A new page requires a distinct service, audience decision or useful task.

Use decision rules that prevent reactive SEO edits

  • Relevant impressions, no useful clicks: first check whether the title and visible promise answer the query accurately. Wait for a meaningful sample before treating CTR as a stable problem.
  • The wrong page matches a useful query: review overlapping copy and internal links between the intended and reported pages. Clarify ownership before creating more content.
  • No reported query: do not convert absence into a demand claim. Confirm indexability and relevance, then continue collecting evidence.
  • An irrelevant query appears: record it as noise unless the business genuinely offers that service. Do not reshape the offer to capture every impression.
  • A page is indexed but receives no enquiries: inspect the complete buyer journey and real contact receipt. This is not automatically a keyword problem.

Keep three measurement streams separate

Search visibility belongs in the verified Search Console property: pages, queries, impressions, clicks and reported average position. Qualified enquiries belong in a private record of received calls, messages or bookings, reviewed for service fit and next step. AI citations, if sampled, need a dated record of the assistant, prompt, response and cited URL.

Do not add these streams into one growth score. An impression is not a visitor, a click is not proof of a received message, and a sampled citation is not a ranking or customer. Each measure supports a different decision.

Download the 28-day review worksheet

Download the Search Console first-28-days worksheet (CSV). It provides checkpoints for approved URLs, inspection findings, page/query signals, visitor next steps and review decisions.

The rows are examples and begin with an unreviewed status. Replace them with your own URLs and verified observations. Keep account exports, customer details and private enquiry records outside a public website repository.

Turn the report into one useful next action

At the end of the review, choose the smallest change supported by the evidence: repair a technical block, clarify an intended service page, strengthen an internal link, correct a redirect or test the enquiry journey. Record the change date, then allow the next comparable period to develop.
